work.title: LANDSCAPE SCAN
work.subtitle: 领域扫描报告
work.scope: Entirely synthetic report exercise: source records, statements and version events are invented. Illustrations are not empirical evidence. No actual study, operational result, market research or participant interview is supplied.

pages.title: Scan a fictional option space.
pages.lead: This report compares six invented prompt-management concepts across four binary feature dimensions. The exercise is a comparison model, not a market survey, competitor benchmark or description of real products.
pages.body: North, Bridge, Grove, Beacon, Harbor and Thread are placeholders. Fifteen of the 24 feature flags are true. A feature count can describe the model but cannot establish quality, value, usability or a winning product.
pages.detail: Separate the supplied synthetic result from your interpretation and any real-world evidence still needed.
pages.question: What decision could this comparison help frame without pretending to be real market research?

pages.title: Declare the scan boundary.
pages.lead: A landscape is shaped by what it includes and excludes. Here the closed set contains six authored concepts, with no external product search or verification.
pages.body: A real scan would need source locations, observation dates, inclusion logic and a plan to revisit changing information. The exported six-row source makes this small fictional boundary inspectable rather than suggesting exhaustive market coverage.

pages.title: Choose consistent dimensions.
pages.lead: The four dimensions are visible version labels, a shared index, an offline copy and a review note. A binary flag means only that the capability is stipulated in the fictional row.
pages.body: True does not mean tested, well implemented or appropriate for a particular user. False means absent in this model, not a verified weakness of a real product. Keep definition questions separate from capability counts.

pages.title: Read the capability matrix.
pages.lead: Version, index and offline flags each appear in four of the six rows. Review-note flags appear in three. The column counts sum to 15 true flags across 24 cells.
pages.body: That total does not mean that 62.5% of an actual market supports these features. It is a property of six authored examples. Keep the denominator and fictional source label beside any summary of the matrix.

pages.title: Map a pair of dimensions.
pages.lead: A two-dimension map is a projection, not the full landscape. Use version visibility and offline copy to show how different configurations can occupy the same region.
pages.body: Bridge and Thread both have version and offline flags. North and Beacon have version without offline; Grove and Harbor have offline without version. No concept occupies neither cell in this particular model. The omitted dimensions still matter.

pages.title: Treat a signal as a hypothesis.
pages.lead: A pattern in the comparison can suggest a question to investigate, but it is not a verified trend. This source has no time series, adoption data or external observations.
pages.body: The combination of offline access and review notes could prompt a design discussion. It cannot be called emerging demand, a growth segment or an underserved market on the basis of these six invented configurations.

pages.title: Mark information gaps honestly.
pages.lead: A binary feature matrix leaves out usability, maintenance, cost, rights and context. Unknown information should stay unknown rather than being filled with assumed ratings.
pages.body: The model supplies no prices, quality tests, product maturity or actual service commitments. A richer real comparison would need relevant sources for each dimension and could reveal that the initial four-feature framing is insufficient.

pages.title: Frame an opportunity without claiming demand.
pages.lead: An apparent empty combination can be a prompt for exploration, not evidence of a valuable opportunity. A concept still needs a coherent purpose and appropriate validation.
pages.body: The model has no row with all four flags, but adding every capability is not automatically a useful design. Context, maintenance and user intent could make a narrower option preferable. No market size or commercial result is supplied.
